sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson, GitHub Copilot will be active in your VS Code installation and you'll have accepted your first AI-generated code suggestion. You'll understand how Copilot works, what the free tier gives you, and the core interaction model: ghost text that appears as you type.

## What GitHub Copilot Is

GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant built directly into VS Code (and other editors). It watches what you type — file name, existing code, and especially your comments — and predicts what you're about to write next. That prediction appears as faded "ghost text" in the editor. Press **Tab** to accept it, or keep typing to ignore it.

Under the hood, Copilot sends your current file context to a large language model (originally OpenAI Codex, now GitHub's own models) and returns a completion. The key difference from a chat AI: Copilot works *inline*, inside your actual code file, without you switching to a browser tab.

**Pricing (as of 2026):**
- **Free tier** — available to all GitHub accounts. Includes a monthly limit of completions and Copilot Chat messages. Enough to use throughout this course.
- **Copilot Pro** — $10/month (or free for verified students via GitHub Education). Unlimited completions, higher Chat limits, access to Claude and GPT-5 models in Chat. Note: from June 2026, premium agent requests use AI Credits ($0.01/credit) on top of the subscription.

For this lesson and the rest of Part 6, the free tier is sufficient.

**GitHub account required.** Copilot is a GitHub product — you sign in with a GitHub account, not an Anthropic or Microsoft account. If you don't have one, create a free account at github.com before continuing. The signup takes under two minutes.

## How Ghost Text Works

The ghost text interaction has three steps:

1. **You type** — a comment, a function signature, or even just a file name gives Copilot context.
2. **Copilot suggests** — faded gray text appears after your cursor. This is the suggestion.
3. **You decide:**
   - **Tab** — accept the full suggestion
   - **Ctrl+Right** — accept one word at a time
   - **Alt+]** — see the next suggestion (Copilot usually has several alternatives)
   - **Alt+[** — see the previous suggestion
   - **Ctrl+Enter** — open a panel showing up to 10 suggestions side by side
   - **Esc** or just keep typing — dismiss the suggestion

The most important habit: **read before you accept.** Ghost text is a proposal, not a command. You are always the decision-maker.

**Comment-driven development:** Copilot's suggestions are only as good as the context you give it. A vague comment like `// helper function` produces a generic suggestion. A specific comment like `// returns the longest word in a string, ignoring punctuation` produces a much more targeted one. Writing clear comments isn't just good practice — it's how you steer the AI.

sections.title: Activate Copilot and Accept Your First Suggestion
sections.content:
**Step 1 — Create a GitHub account and enable Copilot (if you haven't already)**
1. Go to github.com and sign in (or create a free account)
2. Go to github.com/features/copilot and click **Start using Copilot for free**
3. Follow the prompts — no credit card required for the free tier

**Step 2 — Install the GitHub Copilot extension in VS Code**
1. Open VS Code
2. Click the puzzle-piece icon in the Activity Bar (Extensions panel)
3. In the search box, type: `GitHub Copilot`
4. Click the result named **GitHub Copilot** (publisher: GitHub) — NOT "GitHub Copilot Chat" (install both, but start here)
5. Click **Install**
6. A notification appears: **Sign in to use GitHub Copilot** — click it
7. Complete the browser-based sign-in flow (it opens GitHub in your browser)
8. Return to VS Code — the Copilot icon (a small circle) appears in the Status Bar at the bottom

**Step 3 — Also install GitHub Copilot Chat**
1. Back in the Extensions panel, search `GitHub Copilot Chat`
2. Install the one published by GitHub
3. This adds the chat panel (used in lesson 6-3) — install it now while you're here

**Step 4 — Your first suggestion**
1. In the Explorer panel, navigate to `exercises/`
2. Create a new file: `practice.js`
3. On line 1, type this comment exactly:
```
// Function to calculate the average of an array of numbers
```
4. Press Enter and wait 1–2 seconds
5. Copilot's ghost text appears — a complete function in faded gray
6. Press **Tab** to accept it
7. Now press **Ctrl+Enter** — a Copilot Completions panel opens showing alternative suggestions
8. Browse through them — same prompt, different implementations

**You've written code with AI.** The function appeared because your comment was specific. Now try changing the comment to something more vague — watch how the suggestion changes.

sections.title: Workshop A — Quick Skill Drill: Ghost Text Mastery
sections.content:
Practice the full ghost-text keyboard controls in under 10 minutes. Open `exercises/practice.js` in VS Code.

**1. Accept full suggestion (Tab)**
Type: `// Check if a string is a valid email address`
Press Enter, wait for ghost text, press Tab. Inspect the result.

**2. Accept word by word (Ctrl+Right)**
Type: `// Reverse the words in a sentence`
Press Enter, wait for ghost text. Press Ctrl+Right five times — accept the first five words only. Type the rest manually.

**3. Cycle through alternatives (Alt+] and Alt+[)**
Type: `// Convert a hex color code to RGB values`
Press Enter, then Alt+] three times to see three different implementations. Choose the one you like most and press Tab.

**4. Open the completions panel (Ctrl+Enter)**
Type: `// Format a number as currency with dollar sign and two decimal places`
Press Enter, then Ctrl+Enter. The Completions panel opens with up to 10 options. Compare them — which is shortest? Which has best error handling?

**5. AI Review Step**
Select all four functions you just accepted. Open Copilot Chat (Ctrl+Alt+I). Type:
`Review the code we just wrote. Don't validate it — find 3 bugs, edge cases, or improvements.`
Read its response carefully and fix at least one issue it identifies.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build It With AI: String Utility Library
Workshop C — AI-Assisted Debugging: Fix the Broken Utility
Workshop D — Real Project Application: Copilot on Your Own Code
sections.content:
Open a real file from a project you're working on (or use `exercises/string-utils.js` from Workshop B).

**1.** Open the file in VS Code.

**2.** Find a function that could benefit from improvement — something repetitive, poorly named, or missing error handling.

**3.** Place your cursor at the end of that function. Write a comment describing what you want to add:
```javascript
// TODO: Add input validation — throw TypeError if argument is not a string
```
Accept Copilot's implementation.

**4.** Look for a section that is repetitive (same pattern written multiple times). Write a comment before it:
```javascript
// Refactor: extract repeated logic into a reusable helper function
```
Accept the suggestion. Remove the duplicated code.

**5.** At the bottom of the file, write:
```javascript
// Generate JSDoc comments for all functions in this file
```
Accept Copilot's documentation output.

**6.** Save and verify the file still works (run it or open it in a browser).

**Result:** You've applied Copilot to code that actually matters to you — not a toy example.

sections.question: A developer types `// sort` and presses Enter in a JavaScript file. Copilot suggests a generic bubble sort implementation. The developer then rewrites the comment as `// Sort an array of product objects by price ascending, then by name alphabetically if prices are equal` and presses Enter again. What is the most likely outcome?
options: Copilot produces the same generic bubble sort because it ignores comments
Copilot produces a more targeted implementation using a comparator function that handles both sort criteria
Copilot refuses to generate code for complex sort requirements
Copilot generates a sort function but always uses external libraries
sections.explanation: More specific comments produce more targeted suggestions. The detailed comment gives Copilot two explicit sorting criteria (price ascending, then name alphabetically as a tiebreaker), which it can translate directly into a comparator function. The original vague comment produced a generic implementation because Copilot had no constraints to work with.

sections.question: You press Tab to accept a Copilot suggestion and immediately realize it introduced a bug — the function returns undefined instead of the computed value. What should you do first?
options: Undo the acceptance with Ctrl+Z, then examine the ghost text more carefully before re-accepting
Ask Copilot Chat to fix it with /fix
Delete the file and start over
Accept the bug and plan to fix it later
sections.explanation: Ctrl+Z undoes the Tab acceptance, putting you back to the ghost text state. You can then read the suggestion more carefully, use Ctrl+Right to accept word by word to the point where you see the bug, or press Esc to dismiss and write the return statement manually. The undo pattern is the fastest recovery — much faster than fixing a bug after the fact.

sections.question: Which keyboard shortcut opens a panel showing up to 10 alternative Copilot suggestions for the same comment?
sections.explanation: Ctrl+Enter opens the Copilot Completions panel, which displays up to 10 alternative suggestions side by side. This is the best way to compare different approaches Copilot has generated for the same prompt before committing to one. Alt+] only cycles through suggestions one at a time in the inline ghost text view.

sections.content: **Lesson 6-1 complete.** GitHub Copilot is active in your editor. You know how ghost text works, how to navigate multiple suggestions, and why comment quality matters. In lesson 6-2, you'll practice guiding Copilot with precision and learn when to trust its output — and when to verify it.
